entities.summary: Charlemagne (Charles the Great, c. 747–814 CE) was the King of the Franks (768), King of the Lombards (774), and Emperor of the Romans (800) — the first recognized emperor in Western Europe since the fall of Rome in 476 CE. His coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800 CE in St. Peter’s Basilica created the political entity that became the Holy Roman Empire and established the medieval template for the relationship between Church and State. Through 53 military campaigns, he united most of Western Europe under a single ruler for the first time since the Roman Empire: his realm encompassed modern France, Germany, the Low Countries, Switzerland, Austria, northern Italy, and northern Spain. His forced conversion of the pagan Saxons (thirty years of brutal conquest, 772–804 CE) remains controversial — the massacre of 4,500 Saxon prisoners at Verden (782) being the darkest episode. Yet his Carolingian Renaissance revived learning, literacy, and the arts: he established palace schools under Alcuin of York, standardized Carolingian minuscule (the script that evolved into modern lowercase letters), mandated education for clergy, preserved classical texts in monastic scriptoria, and reformed weights, measures, and coinage across his empire. His administrative innovations — the missi dominici (traveling inspectors), county governance, and oath-based loyalty — became the foundation of medieval feudalism. Charlemagne is the common ancestor of virtually every European royal family and most Europeans of European descent. Napoleon called himself ‘the Charlemagne of the modern era,’ and the Charlemagne Prize (Karlspreis) remains Europe’s most prestigious award for contributions to European unity.
